content.comment:
Dear reviewers,

First, we would like to thank the reviewers, who had spent precious time and an enormous effort to review our work. Your feedback showed several drawbacks to the current manuscript. We, therefore, decided to withdraw our paper and will strive to improve it based on your constructive comments.

Sincerely,

Authors

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigates the online-learning generalization risk in the micro-batch setting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
* Online learning is a very practical problem, in real-world applications the labeled data arrive sequentially. (e.g., a system is deployed, and then gets incrementally improved based on annotating the live traffic)

Weakness
* I might be missing something but there seems to be some disconnect between the problem setup and the experiments. In Sec 3.1, the micro-batch online learning is defined as progressively growing the training dataset $D_t = D_{t-1} \bigcup B_t$, where $B_t$ is the micro-batch data. And the generalization bound is derived based on $D_t$. This implies when updating the model at time $t$, the algorithm should be able to sample from both current data batch $B_t$ and all previous data points in $D_{t-1}$. However, in the experiments, at time $t$ the data loader is only allowed to sample from $B_t$ as illustrated by Fig 2.
* While the claim is that the theoretical results from this paper can help practitioners decide how to batch the online data for optimal performance, there is no such discussion of practical guidelines or any concrete example. 
* It is not clear what is different between the analyses for the results with and without label noise. I do not see any assumption made on the type of noise, and there is no noise-related parameter in the bound derived.
* The experiments are super weak. There are many factors that can affect performance and results should be reported with a more comprehensive ablation study. 
* In Fig. 4, what’s causing the performance dip around epoch 50? (Similar things happen in Fig 3 but they are less severe)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity, Quality, and Novelty. Poor
I am not super familiar with online learning, so I did not thoroughly examine the theoretical claims made here. But these results seem rather standard to me. The overall quality suffers because I am unable to get any informed guidance either from the theory, the discussion, or empirical experiments from this paper. Without clarifying the first point I raised in the weakness section, I am unable to make a properly informed evaluation of the novelty of this work. 

Reproducibility. Good
The reported experiments are very simple, and they are unable to justify this study.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies micro-batch online training when learning with both clean and noisy labels. Based on some simple Hoeffding's inequality, they have derived some theoretical bounds of the gaps of empirical risks and gaps of generalization risks. They also conduct some experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 to support their claim.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: This paper is well organized. But currently, the written quality of this paper seems don't meet the standard of ICLR. And the theoretical results are quite doubtful.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Currently, the written quality of this paper seems don't meet the standard of ICLR. And the theoretical results are quite doubtful.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I would recommend a rejection since this paper's written quality doesn't meet the standard of ICLR. The theoretical results are also quite doubtful. In particular, I have the following concerns,

My major concern is the correctness of Theorem1. Since the authors get the classifier $f$ on the training dataset $D_{t}$, the individual loss $L(y_{i}, f(x_{i}))$ will no longer be independent. Therefore, it is not appropriate to simply use Hoffeding's inequality at the bottom of page 5. 

My minor concern is that this paper is not clear enough. 1. In the first line of page 6, it is not "rewritten" but "implies" since the two statements are not equivalent. 2. In algorithm1, it should be $D_{t}$ rather than $D_{i}$. 

Even if Theorem 1 is correct, it only holds for two iterations. If we want to derive some bound for all iterations (which is necessary), the probability of success would be $\Pi_{t}(1 - \delta_{t})$ which will be exponentially small. Besides, this paper assumes that we can get global optimal for each epoch, which is not reasonable. All of these limit the significance of this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper aims to theoretically investigate theoretical guarantees for both (deep) online learning and online learning with noisy labels. The authors first introduce a theoretical bound of the gaps of empirical
risks and gaps of generalization risks in micro-batch online training. Then, they claim that these bounds can help guide the online training scheme. Besides, some experiments are provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Some part of this paper is written rather clearly.
2. This paper considers an interesting learning setting.

Weaknesses:
1. Theoretically, I can not see what the authors want to show, and "the first lower bound" as the authors claimed in their contributions is overclaimed. Specifically, for Theorem 1 and Corollary 1, where the results are not surprising and the proof techniques are standard,
the gaps between these two are probably small and so what? It cannot reflect the final generalization performance.
2. Theoretically, this paper does not consider the specificity of deep learning methods, thus the related claim is highly overclaimed.
3. For learning with noisy labels, the train $\tilde{P}$ and test distribution $P$ are not the same. Thus, the analyses for $\tilde{P}$ in Theorem 2 and Corollary 2 make no sense to reflect the generalization performance for $P$.
4. For Algorithm 1, it seems that this method trains all the dataset $D$ after receiving new micro-batch data. It does not reflect the efficiency of online learning. 
5. For experiments, the results cannot connect with theoretical results.

content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think this paper is bad and the claims are not supported by both theoretical and experimental results.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of establishing theoretical guarantees in the online learning setting where models are updated in real-time as points arrive in a stream. The authors propose bounding the added improvement in the model as it is trained on an additional batch of training data. They also establish a similar result for the case where the labels are noisy. The claim is that this bound can help researchers and practitioners make decisions on the proper number of data to train the model when considering the time for training and computational cost.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
* The problem of online training of models and the theoretical analysis of their learning guarantees are highly relevant and significant to the ML community

## Weaknesses
* Correctness: My main qualm with the paper concerns the correctness of the proposed theoretical results. For instance, Theorem 1 applies to fixed hypotheses $f_t^*$ and $f_{t+B}^*$, but these are a function of the data. So, it seems to me that a supremum over the functions in the hypothesis class have to be considered as is standard in analyses of generalization bounds (see e.g., [1] or more specifically, [2] in particular). But this is not done in Theorem 1 or its proof. Additionally, if we consider a fixed hypothesis as the authors seem to do in the proof, then I don’t see how $P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B)$ for the events surrounding $f_t^*$ and $f_{t+B}^*$, since events $A$ and $B$ are not independent as they both depend on the initial $t$ data points. It would have been correct (regardless of dependence) and much more elegant in terms of the resulting expression to just apply the union bound $P(A \cap B) \ge 1 - (P(\bar A) + P(\bar B))$. I am not sure why that is not done here. My concerns also apply to the other theoretical results in the paper, as their proofs are essentially the same as that of Theorem 1.

* Quality: even if we assume that the theoretical statements and proofs are correct, the paper’s claims and its contents do not align. For instance, the authors state that Theorem 1 allows practitioners and researchers to make decisions on the proper number of data to train the model by allowing them to know in advance the amount of improvement newly arrived data can bring. However, this is not what Theorem 1 provides. It does not follow from Theorem 1 that newly arrived points will decrease the generalization error of the model.

* Originality: the main contribution of the paper which are the theoretical results seem to be straightforward applications of Hoeffding’s theorem twice. To the best of my knowledge, these techniques are not novel and it is not clear that others will benefit from the techniques.

[1] https://cs.nyu.edu/~mohri/mlbook/ 

[2] page 25 of https://cs.nyu.edu/~mohri/mls/ml_learning_with_infinite_hypothesis_sets.pdf
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Please see the Weaknesses section above to comments regarding the quality, clarity, and originality of the work.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors tackle a problem that is very relevant and of high significance to the ML community. However, I have deep concerns about the correctness, novelty, and applicability of the work. The empirical evaluations also seem to be disjoint from what the theory is actually predicting. In light of these considerations, I recommend rejection.

content.title: Theoretical generalization bounds for improving the efficiency of deep online training
content.abstract: In the era of data explosion, online machine learning in which learning models are updated in real-time has become essential due to the growth of data in practice. In particular, it is more challenging to collect and annotate new massive data accurately and timely compared to traditional offline supervised training settings. Although this online training framework has been shown to be practically beneficial, there has been a lack of theoretical guarantees for the learning performance, especially for the case with noisy labels. This paper aims to investigate a learning theory for both original deep online training and online training with noisy labels. We first introduce a theoretical bound of the gaps of empirical risks and gaps of generalization risks in micro-batch online training when learning with both clean and noisy labels. Those bounds will efficiently help guide the online training scheme when receiving new data. We next analyze the impact of micro-batch size on the learning performance of models with noisy labels through our experimental results on CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets using different noise, which consistently demonstrates the merit of the bounds above in the online training setting.
